executive_summary: USD/SGD closed at 1.27819 on 30 October 2026. It is quoted in Singapore dollars per US dollar, so a rising quote means a stronger dollar. The pair fell 0.18% over one month, 0.31% over three months and 1.81% over a year, but rose 0.71% over six months, and it sits at the 36th percentile of its 52-week closing range of 1.26139-1.30791. Bilaterally, the dollar has a stable rate premium of about 258bp over three-month SORA, year-end dollar funding is tightening, and the Singapore dollar is long against its own basket, with MAS adding reserves near the strong side of its band. Against that, Singapore runs a current account surplus near 17% of GDP, MAS keeps a tightening bias and appreciating slope, and the US runs twin deficits of 3.0% and 6.2% of GDP. The standalone dossiers rate the dollar Bullish tactically and the Singapore dollar Neutral. Their negatives mirror each other: the Singapore dollar's tactical drags are funding and band positioning, which are the dollar's tactical positives seen from the other side. The tactical stance is Bullish, conviction 2, score +0.235: the pair leans higher into late November, with a base case of 1.2850 by 27 November. The strategic stance is Bearish, conviction 2, score -0.226: the pair drifts lower from January, towards 1.2620 by end-April 2027. The caveat is that indicative six-month forwards near 1.2627 already price almost exactly that strategic path, so the strategic edge comes from where the trade is entered, ideally selling December rallies into 1.2840-1.2870, not from the direction itself.

market_context.valuation_assessment: On GDP-based PPP the Singapore dollar is about 38% below parity with the dollar, implying USD/SGD near 0.79. The BIS real broad index for the Singapore dollar is 115.04, the 88th percentile of its range since January 2024 and the second-richest in the eleven-currency set. The dollar's index is 107.11, only the 21st percentile. In real trade-weighted terms the Singapore dollar is near the expensive end of its recent history and the dollar near the cheap end. That supports Singapore dollar appreciation at roughly the pace of the band's slope (about 1.25% a year), not faster. The current level prices an unchanged appreciating band and a Fed that hikes once more. bilateral_carry_analysis.carry_assessment: Annualised carry is about +258bp for a long USD/SGD position: the Fed target mid-point of 3.875% against three-month compounded SORA of 1.297%. On SOFR of 3.94% it is about 264bp. Singapore has no policy rate; under free capital movement SORA sits below US rates by roughly the expected appreciation. This is a policy and money-market gap, not a measured forward funding differential, because no Singapore dollar future is listed. The carry-to-implied-volatility ratio cannot be computed because no implied volatility exists; on 60-day realised volatility of 2.89% the carry-to-realised ratio is about 0.89, the highest dollar carry-to-volatility ratio in the set, but that is a realised-basis measure and not the standard one. Carry is working only partly: indicative bank forward points from mid-October (1M -19, 3M -73, 6M -155 pips) put about 1.8%, 2.3% and 2.4% a year of Singapore dollar appreciation into the forwards, roughly equal to the money-market gap, so a long USD/SGD position earns carry only to the extent that spot outperforms the forward.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: On 28 October the Federal Reserve held its target range at 3.75-4.00% by a 10-2 vote. Two governors dissented in favour of an immediate hike, and futures put the chance of a 25bp increase at the 9 December meeting at 77-85%. Singapore has no policy rate. MAS steers the S$NEER inside an undisclosed band and left the slope, width and centre unchanged on 14 October, so the domestic short rate is an output of that regime: three-month compounded SORA is 1.297%. The bilateral gap is therefore about 258bp against the Fed mid-point, or about 264bp using SOFR at 3.94%, and a long USD/SGD position earns it. Nothing scheduled in the next four weeks changes that gap. The 9 December FOMC, which brings new projections, falls just after the tactical window, and no MAS decision is on the verified schedule for the period. The effect works mainly through the dollar leg. MAS manages the Singapore dollar against a basket, so USD/SGD moves when the dollar moves against that basket. If firm November data keep the Fed premium in place, the dollar stays supported against the low-yielding basket currencies. The offset is the band's slope, estimated at about 1.25% a year, which lifts the trade-weighted Singapore dollar by roughly 0.1% a month and absorbs part of any dollar gain. We lean Bullish at low confidence because the gap is wide and stable, not widening.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the question is whether the gap widens or narrows, and the dated test is the 9 December FOMC with its Summary of Economic Projections. The market prices a Fed path of about 4.7% by September 2027 against a median dot of 4.1%. The strategic risk on the dollar leg is therefore a downward repricing if the projections confirm one more hike followed by a hold. On the Singapore side, SORA follows US dollar rates only partly and with a lag: the three-month rate rose from a 1.06% average in the second quarter to about 1.30% now. A December hike would therefore widen the money-market gap towards 280-300bp unless SORA catches up. MAS kept the appreciating slope and said risks to inflation remain tilted to the upside. That rules out a near-term easing of the band and gives the Singapore dollar a steady anchor of about 0.6% trade-weighted appreciation by end-April. The net picture is a wide gap that may widen a little if the hike is delivered, but markets already price more than the median dot, while the band keeps appreciating whatever the Fed does. A hike with projections signalling a hold would hurt the dollar against the priced path; a hike with higher dots would help it. We cannot call that outcome with confidence before 9 December, so we hold Neutral.

carry_analysis.note: Annualised carry 257.8bp, earned by a long USD/SGD position (long US dollar, short Singapore dollar). Basis: Fed target mid-point 3.875% against 3M compounded SORA 1.297%; about 264bp on SOFR 3.94%. This is a policy-rate and money-market gap, not a measured forward funding differential: no SGD future is listed. Carry-to-vol ratio not computable: no exchange lists an option on the Singapore dollar, so no 3M implied volatility exists (about 0.89 on 60-day realised vol of 2.89%, a realised-basis measure only). Carry regime: carry favours the dollar leg, but under MAS's appreciating band it is offset by expected trade-weighted Singapore dollar appreciation of about 1.25% a year; indicative bank forwards from mid-October put about 2.3-2.4% a year of SGD appreciation into the forward, roughly equal to the money-market gap, so carry pays the holder only if spot outperforms the forward. Breakeven: at about 258bp a year a long earns roughly 0.21% a month (about 27 pips a month), or about 1.3% over six months, before spot moves against it erase the carry.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The growth gap favours Singapore firmly. Third-quarter GDP rose 5.4% y/y and 1.1% q/q, against 2.07% y/y and 3.4% annualised in the US. September non-oil domestic exports rose 68.4% y/y, and unemployment is 2.0% against 4.2%. The inflation gap points the other way for policy: US core PCE is 3.1% y/y and headline CPI 3.7%, while MAS core inflation eased to 2.0%, inside MAS's 1.5-2.0% range for 2026. The two sides do not move the pair equally. Singapore's data feed MAS's reaction function, but the band absorbs domestic surprises and no MAS decision falls in the window, so strong prints confirm the existing slope rather than changing pricing. US data, by contrast, move Fed pricing directly. Payrolls on 6 November and October CPI on 10 November will decide whether December odds hold at 77-85%. Activity and price surveys point to firm prints, while a soft labour market is the downside risk: September payrolls rose only 29,000, with 60,000 of downward revisions. The two effects offset. Singapore's lead is real but will not move the pair for four weeks, and US data are most likely to confirm what is already priced. We hold Neutral.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months both economies slow. MAS expects the positive output gap to narrow through 2027 and core inflation to ease noticeably from mid-2027. Singapore's export growth also faces a very high base as the AI surge laps itself. In the US, the Fed projects core PCE falling to 2.5% in 2027, real average hourly earnings are falling, and three-month average payroll growth is only about 51,000, which makes the labour market the most likely source of a surprise. Singapore keeps the better mix of growth and inflation. But MAS has signalled no case for a steeper band, so its data lead will not turn into a policy change before its next statement. The US side is more two-sided. Sticky inflation would validate the market's hawkish path, while unemployment rising towards 4.5% would pull Fed pricing down sharply and weaken the dollar against the basket the Singapore dollar tracks. That leaves a slight skew against the dollar, but too small to give a stance, so we hold Neutral.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: USD/SGD is not very sensitive to risk appetite. The Singapore dollar acts as a regional anchor: it weakens modestly against the dollar in global risk-off and outperforms higher-beta Asian and G10 currencies. Risk appetite is cautious rather than stressed. The VIX closed at 17.2 on 29 October and traded near 20 intraday on 30 October, and US investment-grade and high-yield spreads were at 89bp and 326bp after an AI-led equity sell-off. The usual link, where risk-off lifts the pair through a dollar bid, is weaker than normal: the dollar index fell on the 30 October sell-off as the yen and franc absorbed haven demand. Both legs share the same specific risk. AI capital spending drives US equity leadership and also Singapore's electronics exports, so a deeper technology correction hurts the US growth-exceptionalism story and Singapore's growth story at once. China's third-quarter growth of 4.5% removes the regional stress channel that has historically mattered for the Singapore dollar. With the dollar's haven bid muted and an AI shock hitting both sides, we hold Neutral.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the risk tails are wide but point both ways for this pair. A deeper AI-led equity correction would hit US assets first and could trigger dollar selling as underhedged foreign holders raise their hedge ratios. The same correction would hurt Singapore's export engine, which MAS itself lists as a downside risk. An escalation in the Gulf would lift oil and push the dollar towards the left side of the smile against an oil-importing Singapore dollar. A settlement would cut oil and improve Asian growth and capital flows, which favours the Singapore dollar. Credit spreads are wider than a year ago but still low compared with stress episodes, so the system can absorb a shock. The band caps how far the Singapore dollar can move in either direction, which shrinks the net effect of any of these outcomes on the pair. We hold Neutral at low confidence.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Neither leg gives a clean futures reading for this pair. There is no reportable Singapore dollar contract, so positioning has to be built from dollar futures and from where the S$NEER sits in MAS's band. On the dollar side, leveraged funds are moderately long. They were net long 3,158 ICE dollar-index contracts in the week to 27 October and about USD 15.9bn long the dollar across the six CME currency futures. That is the 83rd-87th percentile of a year but only the 57th-71st of five years, so the long is building but not crowded. On the Singapore side, OCBC's model puts the S$NEER about 1.65% above the band mid-point, down from 1.85% before the 14 October hold. Trade-weighted Singapore dollar length is therefore in the upper part of a band commonly estimated at plus or minus 2%, with more room to slip than to extend. MAS appears to be leaning against strength: official reserves rose S$2.84bn in September to S$553.57bn, the highest since 2022, consistent with buying dollars near the strong side of the band. Taken together, moderate dollar length meets a Singapore dollar that is long against its basket and capped by its own central bank, which tilts flows towards a firmer USD/SGD over four weeks. Confidence is low because both readings are proxies.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the slow flows matter more than the fast ones. The band's mid-point rises about 0.6% by end-April at the estimated slope, which absorbs today's trade-weighted Singapore dollar length without any need for it to unwind. On the dollar side, the structural flows lean negative. The dollar's share of allocated reserves fell to 56.70% in the second quarter, and foreign holdings of Treasury bills fell USD 47.8bn in August. ING flags low hedge ratios on US assets as the main dollar risk, and that risk grows as the Fed nears its peak and hedging becomes cheaper. Singapore is a major Asian wealth and asset-management hub, and its large official and private holders of US assets are exactly the investors whose hedge ratios would rise. Asset managers have held foreign-currency futures longs of about USD 7.9bn through the autumn, which shows real money has not joined the dollar rally. We are mildly Bearish: the dollar faces slow but persistent supply from hedging and diversification, while the Singapore dollar's basket length is absorbed rather than reversed.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The structural gap is large. Singapore's current account surplus was 16.7% of GDP in 2025 and S$37.08bn in the second quarter of 2026. The US deficit widened to 3.0% of GDP and its net international investment position stands at -USD 22.42tn. Direct goods trade between the two does not carry that imbalance, however. IMF trade data for 2024 show US exports to Singapore of $46.0bn against imports of $43.2bn, a US goods surplus of $2.8bn, and Singapore's own figures show it importing $55.9bn from the US against $44.1bn of exports. Singapore earns its surplus against the rest of the world, and MAS, GIC and Temasek recycle it, so it supports the Singapore dollar through the basket rather than through direct USD/SGD flows. Terms of trade currently favour the dollar. The US is a net energy exporter and Singapore a net crude importer, and Brent rose about 15% in October to US$117.64, though Singapore's refining and re-export margins partly hedge that. Over four weeks the oil channel and the surplus roughly cancel, so we hold Neutral.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the external gap is the strongest structural argument against the pair. A surplus near 17% of GDP is a continuous net supply of foreign currency that MAS recycles through an appreciating band. The third-quarter balance of payments, due in late November, is likely to exceed the second quarter's S$37.08bn given how much exports accelerated. The US runs twin deficits: a current account gap of 3.0% of GDP and a budget deficit of 6.2%. Its investment position worsened by USD 1.15tn in a single quarter, so the deficit stays easily financed only while US yields keep their premium. As the Fed nears its peak and peers tighten, investors demand more compensation, and that is when an external deficit starts to weigh on a currency. Oil is the main offset: a prolonged Hormuz disruption would widen Singapore's import bill and favour the energy-exporting US. The US goods surplus with Singapore also means direct trade gives the Singapore dollar no extra lift. Tariff risk on AI hardware, Singapore's main export to the US, is the other tail. We are Bearish on the pair, with the highest strategic confidence of any factor.

factors.horizon_split: Neutral tactically because the oil terms-of-trade channel, which favours the dollar, cancels the slow-acting surplus over four weeks. Bearish strategically because the surplus and deficit build up through flows, while the US yield premium that finances the deficit narrows as peers tighten. The weight rises from 0.06 to 0.16, making this the largest strategic driver. Bilateral investment context: the capital account runs heavily in both directions. US direct investment stock in Singapore reached $424 billion in 2023. The United States made up 39% of GIC's portfolio, and industry estimates put GIC's managed assets above $700 billion. That concentration is why the hedge-ratio channel in Factor 4 matters for this pair specifically: Singapore's official and private holders of US assets are large enough that a change in their hedging moves forward dollar supply.

net_commodity_exposure.base_commodity_profile: US: net energy exporter of crude and natural gas, with Henry Hub gas cheap at about US$2.76. Higher oil is mildly positive for the dollar through terms of trade against energy importers.
net_commodity_exposure.quote_commodity_profile: Singapore: net crude importer and a regional refining, bunkering and re-export hub. Under the direction rules higher oil is negative for the Singapore dollar, partly hedged by refining margins; higher LNG (JKM) prices are also negative.
net_commodity_exposure.net_effect_calculation: If oil rises, the dollar gets a mild positive (+) as a net energy exporter whose terms of trade improve against importers. The Singapore dollar gets a negative (-) as a net crude importer; the direction rules group it with the euro and sterling among the losers. Netting a positive for the base against a negative for the quote gives a positive effect on the pair: USD/SGD rises. The effect is small for two reasons. Singapore's complex refining margin jumped to about US$30 a barrel when the Hormuz disruption began, offsetting part of the import bill. And the MAS band absorbs imported-inflation shocks by keeping the slope appreciating, which leans against Singapore dollar weakness. Higher LNG prices add a further mild negative for the Singapore dollar.
net_commodity_exposure.scenario_oil_up_10pct: Mildly positive for the pair. US terms of trade improve and Singapore's import bill rises. Higher imported inflation, however, strengthens MAS's upside-risk bias and keeps the band appreciating, which offsets part of the move.
net_commodity_exposure.scenario_oil_down_10pct: Mildly negative for the pair. An oil fall, most plausibly from a US-Iran settlement, improves Singapore's terms of trade and Asian growth, removes part of the dollar's energy advantage and lowers US inflation risk.
net_commodity_exposure.dominant_commodity_driver: Crude oil through the Strait of Hormuz. For Singapore the dominant non-commodity external driver is the AI-electronics export cycle.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Both central banks are credible and both messages are already known. The Fed's 28 October statement was hawkish, with two dissents for an immediate hike, but Chair Warsh declined to pre-judge December and said he does not believe in forward guidance outside a crisis, which leaves the market to follow the data. MAS's 14 October statement held the band while saying risks to inflation remain tilted to the upside. It was a hawkish hold, but it surprised OCBC, DBS and ING, which had expected another slight slope increase. The gap between the two banks' guidance is small: if anything both lean towards tightening, the Fed openly through its dissenters and MAS implicitly through its risk language. The only scheduled communication in the next four weeks is the FOMC minutes on 18 November, which will show how broad the hawkish wing is. No MAS communication is on the verified schedule for the period. Pricing is already ahead of the Fed's median and forwards assume MAS holds, so neither bank's guidance can shift the pair within the window. Neutral.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the guidance asymmetry favours the Singapore dollar. MAS's next change, if any, is more likely a tightening than an easing. It tightened in April and July 2026 when imported inflation rose, it describes the band as leaning against an expected rise in imported inflation, and Brent above US$110 keeps that channel live. The Fed's credibility is high, but its guidance has less room to surprise on the hawkish side. The market already prices a path about 60bp above the median dot, so the 9 December projections are more likely to pull the priced path down than push it up. They will be the first under the Chair's no-guidance approach. A Fed that confirms one more hike and then a hold, while MAS keeps an appreciating slope with a tightening bias, is the combination that moves the pair lower. We are Bearish at modest confidence because the next MAS statement is not on the verified schedule and the December projections could still surprise upward.

Strategically, MAS's upside-risk language and a Fed path priced above the dots make the next surprise more likely to favour the Singapore dollar, so the factor turns Bearish for the pair.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The event calendar is concentrated on the dollar leg. The 3 November midterms, where a Democratic House is close to fully priced, open a window in which the US has signalled strikes on Iran could resume. A strike would lift oil and most likely the dollar against the oil-importing Singapore dollar, while a Qatari-brokered ceasefire would do the reverse. We put about 20% on a strike within four weeks and 15% on a ceasefire, a slight skew in the dollar's favour. On the other side, ING warns that a Republican loss of the House could push the administration back towards trade action, which it sees as negative for the dollar. Singapore is unusually exposed to any extension of US tariffs to AI hardware, since its exports to the US rose 73.2% in September. Domestic political risk in Singapore is negligible. The skews roughly cancel, so we hold Neutral.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months three branches dominate. First, the Gulf. A US-Iran deal, which we put at about 25% within six months, would remove the energy premium that favours the dollar over oil importers and would support Asian growth and flows into the Singapore dollar. A sustained closure of Hormuz, at about 15%, would raise Singapore's import bill and lift the dollar. Second, US trade policy. A divided Congress may push the administration towards tariffs, which would hit Singapore's AI-hardware exports, but tariffs were negative for the dollar through confidence in US assets in 2025. Third, US fiscal deadlines: government funding expires on 11 December, and a Democratic House from January raises the risk of shutdowns in 2027. US-China technology controls are a slower-burning risk to Singapore's role in the semiconductor supply chain. These branches offset, so we hold Neutral.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The fiscal gap is among the widest in the group. The US federal deficit was USD 2.0tn in FY2026, or 6.2% of GDP. Debt held by the public is about 100% of GDP, interest costs are about 3.4% of GDP, and the US is rated AA+ by S&P and Fitch and Aa1 by Moody's, all with stable outlooks. Singapore ended FY2025 with a surplus of 1.9% of GDP, projects 1.0% for FY2026, is rated AAA by all three agencies, and funds a sixth of its budget from reserve returns. No event in the next four weeks is likely to put that gap into the price. Treasury's quarterly refunding on 4 November is expected to leave coupon sizes unchanged, and the 11 December funding deadline falls just after the window. Singapore's next fiscal event is its February budget. A gap this wide is a permanent, priced feature rather than a four-week driver, so we hold Neutral.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the fiscal gap becomes a slow negative for the dollar. A 6.2%-of-GDP deficit outside a recession, rising interest costs as low-coupon debt rolls over, and S&P's warning that the rating could slip within two years if deficits rise leave little fiscal room. The lame-duck Congress must extend funding by 11 December, and a Democratic House from January raises the odds of budget fights in 2027. The bond market has begun to charge for this through a term premium that has so far supported the dollar by lifting yields. But a sharper fiscal premium that is not matched by higher policy expectations would reverse that link. Singapore sits at the other extreme: a AAA surplus backed by large reserves, so its fiscal space removes any downside tail for its currency if the AI cycle turns. As peers' fiscal premia rise, Singapore's scarcity value grows at the margin. We are Bearish on the pair at modest confidence because the deterioration is gradual and demand for Treasuries remains deep.

factors.horizon_split: Neutral tactically because no fiscal event falls inside four weeks. Bearish strategically because the US deficit, interest burden and 2027 political calendar build into term-premium risk once the Fed stops hiking, while Singapore's surplus becomes a relative advantage.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: USD/SGD is a managed cross. MAS steers the S$NEER inside an undisclosed band, so the pair's behaviour is set by the dollar's moves against Singapore's basket and by where the S$NEER sits in the band, not by a freely floating order book. That structure gives the pair the lowest realised volatility of any dollar pair we follow: about 2.4% over 20 days and 2.9% over 60. It also tends to keep the pair contained between policy events. No exchange lists an option on the Singapore dollar, so implied volatility, risk reversals and the volatility term structure cannot be taken from any venue we can name, and the gap between implied and realised volatility cannot be measured. With the S$NEER about 1.65% above the mid-point, the band's strong edge is nearer than its weak edge, which limits how far the pair can fall on a dollar sell-off before MAS leans against it. With no Singapore policy event in the window and volatility pinned low, the structure favours a contained pair rather than a trending one. Neutral.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the structure stays one of low volatility inside a managed regime, and volatility is likely to rise only around a change in MAS's band. The January and April 2025 easing moves shifted the pair by more than 1% within weeks, and the next MAS statement is not on the verified schedule. The slope adds a slow, steady downward pull on the pair of about 0.1% a month, provided the dollar is broadly flat against the basket and the S$NEER holds its position in the band. Any directional move bigger than that has to come from the dollar leg or from MAS. Low realised volatility makes options on a managed currency usually look expensive relative to recent moves, but without a quote we cannot confirm that. The structure sets the pace of any move, not its direction, so we hold Neutral.

It moves into the 1.2976-1.30751 resistance band by early March 2027, which hardens the ceiling over any rebound in the first half of 2027.

No venue quotes implied volatility, so the cost of options cannot be measured. The regime suits carry and forwards rather than paying for optionality.
expression_assessment.directional_expression: Spot or forwards are the natural tools. Tactically, a long USD/SGD forward collects the roughly 258bp money-market gap while waiting. Strategically, a short-dollar view pays that carry away, so it needs spot to fall faster than the forward discount, and crosses where the Singapore dollar's carry cost is lower are more efficient ways to express Singapore dollar strength.
expression_assessment.event_timing_consideration: The 9 December FOMC with projections is the only verified scheduled policy decision for either leg before March and the most likely date for the pair to reprice. MAS's next statement is not on the verified schedule, and a band change would be the largest volatility event for the pair.
expression_assessment.liquidity_note: The Singapore dollar is the most actively traded currency in Southeast Asia and spot and forward markets are deep onshore and in Asian hours. There is no exchange-listed future or option, however, so execution is over the counter and liquidity thins outside Asian trading hours and around year-end.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Dollar liquidity is tightening into year-end. Reserve balances fell USD 68.8bn in the week to 28 October to an average of USD 2,893.8bn as the Treasury General Account rose above USD 1tn, ahead of Treasury's USD 850bn end-December target. SOFR at 3.94% sits 4bp above the interest paid on reserve balances. The Fed's balance sheet is flat and reserve management purchases have been zero since mid-August, so nothing offsets the drain. Singapore is the hub of the Asian dollar market, and its banks and corporates run large dollar books funded offshore. A higher marginal cost of dollars therefore passes quickly into the forward market and into demand for dollars against the Singapore dollar. There is no sign of stress: the standing repo facility was used for only USD 6m and central bank swap lines for USD 156m. No venue publishes the SGD/USD cross-currency basis, so this is an argument about the cost of funding, not about stress. Over four weeks it leans the pair higher, at low confidence.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the Fed is likely to respond to any reserve scarcity rather than let funding tighten. The Desk is authorised to buy bills and short coupons to keep reserves ample, it ran reserve management purchases earlier in the year, and Treasury's planned fall in the TGA to USD 850bn by end-December would return about USD 165bn of reserves in early 2027. Seasonal year-end demand for dollars in Asia normally fades by mid-January. On the Singapore side, MAS's reserves of S$553.57bn give it ample capacity to supply dollars if the band's weak side were tested, so a funding squeeze cannot push the Singapore dollar far. The SORA-SOFR gap may widen if the Fed hikes, but that is a rates question already scored under Policy & Rates. Tightness into year-end and easing afterwards roughly offset over the horizon, so we hold Neutral.

Neutral strategically because the TGA's planned decline and the Fed's readiness to buy bills should restore ample reserves after December.

tactical.score_interpretation: A score of +0.235 is Bullish under the rule, but it comes from breadth, not depth. Three low-confidence factors, all on the dollar leg, do the work: Policy & Rates (+0.125), USD Liquidity (+0.058) and Flows & Positioning (+0.052). The other seven are Neutral, none is Bearish, and no factor has confidence above 53%. The decisive rates event, the 9 December FOMC with projections, falls just after the four-week window, so the score describes a pair leaning higher on a stable rate premium and year-end funding, not one being pushed by a dated catalyst.
tactical.rationale: At tactical weights, Policy & Rates (0.24), Inflation & Growth (0.18) and USD Liquidity (0.11) carry more than half the score. Two of them lean towards a firmer USD/SGD and the third is Neutral. The rate channel adds +0.125: the dollar earns about 258bp over three-month SORA, and futures price a December hike at 77-85%, while MAS left its band unchanged on 14 October and has no decision on the verified schedule in the window. Year-end dollar funding adds +0.058: reserves fell USD 68.8bn in a week as the TGA rose above USD 1tn, and Singapore's role as the Asian dollar hub passes that cost straight into the forward market. Positioning adds +0.052: moderate leveraged dollar length meets a Singapore dollar held near the strong side of its band, with MAS adding S$2.84bn of reserves in September. Inflation & Growth is Neutral, because Singapore's 5.4% growth and 68.4% export surge cannot move a band-managed currency before MAS meets again, while US data mostly confirm what is priced. The net is +0.235, Bullish at conviction 2. The two standalone views fit together. Our dollar view is Bullish (+0.326) and our Singapore dollar view is Neutral (+0.015), and the Singapore dollar's own negatives, funding and band positioning, are the dollar's positives seen from the other side. The pair-specific factor that tempers the call is the band: its slope lifts the trade-weighted Singapore dollar about 0.1% a month and absorbs part of any dollar gain. What is priced is a December hike and a quiet year-end. Our edge is that funding pressure lifts SOFR above the rate paid on reserves, which is not priced. The path of least resistance is a modest firming of the pair through November rather than a trend. The dated tests are the midterms on 3 November, payrolls on 6 November, October CPI on 10 November, the FOMC minutes on 18 November and Singapore's October trade and inflation data in the second half of November, with the 9 December projections just beyond the window. Conviction is 2, not 3, because the score rests on three factors at 52-53% confidence and none of them is dated inside the window. A soft payroll or CPI print would remove the rate leg and most of the score with it. Where the levels sit against the call: the chart does not contradict the Bullish lean, but it does limit the payoff. Spot sits 3 pips under the 200-day and 30 pips under the lower edge of the seven-touch 1.2812-1.29395 resistance band. Two local desks read the next few weeks as two-way: UOB holds a 1.2775-1.2835 range and OCBC sees mildly bearish daily momentum. A realistic base-case gain is therefore 30-40 pips on spot, and in this trade carry earns roughly as much as the expected spot move.
tactical.g10_relative_ranking: Our standalone scores rank the dollar 1st of 11 tactically and the Singapore dollar 6th, so long USD/SGD is a mid-table dollar long. The score gap between its legs, about +0.31, is roughly half that of short EUR/USD or short NZD/USD, where the gap is about +0.6. It also trails long USD/CHF, where the carry is wider and the franc ranks lower. Among dollar longs against Asian currencies it is lower-beta and cheaper to hold than long USD/JPY, which faces an official intervention cap, but its expected move is smaller because MAS's band absorbs part of any dollar strength.

External Balance subtracts 0.093: Singapore's surplus near 17% of GDP is a continuous supply of foreign currency recycled through an appreciating band, while the US runs a 3.0%-of-GDP current account deficit and a 6.2%-of-GDP budget deficit, and its investment position worsened by USD 1.15tn in one quarter. Guidance subtracts 0.064: MAS says risks to inflation are tilted to the upside, so its next band change is more likely a tightening, while the market prices a Fed path about 60bp above the median dot, so the 9 December projections are more likely to disappoint than surprise on the hawkish side. Fiscal subtracts 0.039 on a AAA surplus against rising US term-premium risk, and Flows subtract 0.031 as reserve diversification and higher hedge ratios on US assets add slow dollar supply. Policy & Rates is Neutral: the 258bp gap may widen on a December hike, but the market already prices more than the dots. The net is -0.226, Bearish at conviction 2. The standalone views agree: our dollar view is Neutral with a bearish tilt (-0.096) and our Singapore dollar view is Bullish (+0.138). The pair-specific point is that the US runs a small goods surplus with Singapore, so Singapore's surplus helps its currency through the basket and MAS's recycling, not through direct trade. What is priced matters most here. Forwards already discount about 2.4% a year of Singapore dollar appreciation, so the bearish spot view largely coincides with the forward, and the edge against the forward is thin. The path of least resistance is a pair that stays firm into the December FOMC and year-end funding, then drifts lower from January as funding normalises and the slope reasserts. The dated catalysts are the 9 December FOMC projections, the 11 December US funding deadline, Singapore's third-quarter balance of payments in late November, and MAS's next statement, which banks expect in late January but which is not on the verified schedule. Conviction is 2 because the factors are slow, the forward has captured much of the move, and an oil escalation or hawkish December dots would undercut the call. Where the levels sit against the call: the bearish spot view has a structural ally on the chart. The 200-week average sits 396 pips overhead, has capped every close for 90 weeks, and moves into the 1.2976-1.30751 resistance band by early March, so rebounds face a hardening ceiling. The view's weakness is entry, not direction. Selling at today's 1.2782 against a forward near 1.2627 earns almost nothing if the base case of 1.2620 is reached, which is why the plan waits for December strength.
strategic.g10_relative_ranking: Over one to three months our standalone scores rank the Singapore dollar 3rd of 11 and the dollar 6th, so short USD/SGD is a moderate Singapore dollar long with a score gap of about 0.23. It is not the cleanest way to own the Singapore dollar: against the euro, which ranks last strategically, the gap is wider and the carry cost about half as large. Among dollar shorts, USD/JPY and USD/SEK rank ahead because the yen and krona rank 1st and 2nd. Short USD/SGD's appeal is stability: it is the lowest-volatility dollar short in the set, but forwards already price most of the expected move.

strategic.path_expectation: The path runs in three phases. November to December: the pair stays firm in 1.2780-1.2870, supported by year-end dollar funding and the December FOMC; this is the window to build the position. Mid-January: reserves are rebuilt as the TGA falls towards USD 850bn, and MAS's January statement, expected but not confirmed for late January, should keep the slope; the pair should then slip through 1.2740, the top of the seven-touch support band, by February. March and April: a grind of about 30 pips a month, in line with the slope, carries the pair through the band towards 1.2620-1.2640, and the April statement is the final test. Pullbacks towards 1.2780-1.2800 are likely on oil spikes and should fade under a declining 200-week average. Realised volatility should stay at 2.5-3.5%, with a jump only if MAS changes the slope. The pattern is a grind, not a step.

risk_reward.base_case_payoff: +162 pips (+1.27%) from spot 1.27819 to 1.2620 (short); against the indicative 6M forward of 1.2627 only +7 pips
risk_reward.downside_case_loss: -161 pips (pair-higher case at 1.2980) from spot; -353 pips against the 6M forward
risk_reward.risk_reward_ratio: About 1:1 from spot (+162 base vs -161 pair-higher case); from a 1.2855 entry the base case pays +111 against -249 in the pair-higher case
risk_reward.expected_value: Spot EV = 0.50 × 162 + 0.25 × 302 - 0.25 × 161 = +116 pips. Against the 6M forward of 1.2627: base +7, pair-lower +147, pair-higher -353, EV = 3.5 + 36.75 - 88.25 = -48 pips; carrying a short from today is negative expected value because the forward already holds the move. From a 1.2855 entry with about 124 pips of carry to end-April (effective forward near 1.2731): +111 (base), +251 (pair-lower), -249 (pair-higher); EV = 55.5 + 62.75 - 62.25 = +56 pips.
risk_reward.asymmetry_assessment: From spot the asymmetry is unfavourable because of carry. From a December rally entry it turns modestly favourable, because the stop sits beneath a hardening long-term ceiling and the pair-lower tail (a MAS tightening) is not priced. Execution: sell USD/SGD forwards on rallies into 1.2840-1.2870 between the 9 December FOMC and mid-January; stop on a weekly close above 1.2980, about 125 pips from a 1.2855 entry, set inside the three-touch band and under the falling 200-week average; targets 1.2620, then 1.2480. Sizing: conviction 2 means half the standard risk unit, for example 0.25% of capital at risk on a 0.97% stop, a notional of about 0.26 times capital.

consensus_divergence.bank_consensus_forecast: No multi-bank survey for USD/SGD in free sources; individual banks: ING (12 October) 1.28 at one and three months, 1.27 at six and 1.26 at twelve; BofA 1.30 by December 2026, then 1.28 in September 2027, with a call for calibrated MAS tightening in January 2027; MUFG USD/SGD 1.26 by Q3 2027; OCBC keeps a constructive medium-term Singapore dollar outlook while near-term direction stays sensitive to the dollar, Treasury yields and the renminbi.
consensus_divergence.bank_consensus_forecast_source: ING (FX Talking, October 2026), BofA, MUFG, OCBC: individual bank research as reported in FX commentary
consensus_divergence.our_tactical_view: Bullish, base case USD/SGD 1.2850 by 27 November 2026
consensus_divergence.our_strategic_view: Bearish, base case USD/SGD 1.2620 by 30 April 2027
consensus_divergence.divergence_direction: Tactical above ING's one-month 1.28 and below BofA's December 1.30; strategic below ING's six-month 1.27 and in line with MUFG's 1.26 but reaching it earlier
consensus_divergence.divergence_magnitude: Tactical 1.2850 is +50 pips above ING's one-month 1.28 and 150 pips below BofA's December 1.30; strategic 1.2620 is 80 pips below ING's six-month 1.27 and reaches MUFG's 1.26 about five months earlier
consensus_divergence.why_we_differ: We differ on drivers, not direction. Near term we put more weight on year-end dollar funding and MAS's reserve buying than ING's flat one-month number allows. Over six months we put more weight on the external balance and MAS's tightening bias than BofA does. An independent (non-bank) forecaster, Cambridge Currencies, sees 1.26-1.30 to end-2026 and 1.25-1.31 over six months.
consensus_divergence.payoff_if_right: About 70 pips plus carry on a tactical long, then about 110 pips net of carry on a strategic short entered near 1.2855.
consensus_divergence.risk_if_wrong: BofA's 1.30 on the tactical side would stop out a December short entry near 1.2980. On the strategic side, ING's 1.27 would leave a short-dollar forward from today's spot paying about 165 pips of carry to make roughly 80.

cross_horizon_consistency.explanation: The horizons diverge because different factors dominate. Over four weeks the heaviest live influences are the dollar's rate premium, which no scheduled decision can disturb before 9 December, tightening year-end dollar funding, and MAS leaning against a Singapore dollar near the strong side of its band. Over one to three months the weights shift towards External Balance, Guidance and Fiscal, where Singapore's surplus, MAS's tightening bias and the US twin deficits all favour a lower pair, while year-end funding pressure fades.
cross_horizon_consistency.inflection_point: Between the 9 December FOMC projections and early January 2027, when year-end dollar funding pressure normally fades. MAS's next statement, which banks expect in late January, is not on the verified schedule and would be a second inflection if it changes the band.
cross_horizon_consistency.trading_implication: Favour dollar-positive tactical exposure into the December FOMC through positions that collect the carry, and reassess after the projections. Build the strategic Singapore dollar view after year-end funding fades. The forward discount already embeds about 2.4% a year of Singapore dollar appreciation, so a short-dollar position needs spot to fall faster than the forward implies, and crosses with lower carry cost may express the view more efficiently. In practice, the tactical long's target zone of 1.2840-1.2870 is also the strategic short's entry zone, so the hand-over between the two views is a single level, not just a date.

catalysts.rationale: A Democratic House is about 94% priced. The result opens the window in which the US has signalled strikes on Iran could resume; a strike would lift oil and the pair. ING warns that a Republican loss of the House could revive trade policy, which is negative for the dollar and a risk to Singapore's AI-hardware exports.

Treasury plans USD 628bn of fourth-quarter borrowing and is expected to keep coupon sizes unchanged. A surprise increase would lift the US term premium for fiscal reasons, which in this regime is more likely to weaken the dollar against a AAA-surplus currency than to support it through yield.

Consensus is +55,000 payrolls with 4.2% unemployment after a 29,000 September gain and 60,000 of revisions. A firm print holds December hike pricing and the dollar's rate premium behind the tactical view; a negative print would remove the rate leg of the score.

September core CPI rose 0.3% m/m with a 3.4% three-month annualised pace. A repeat would lock in December hike pricing and the dollar's premium over the Singapore dollar's low-yielding basket. A soft print would weaken the dollar leg, and with it the pair.

catalysts.event: Singapore October non-oil domestic exports (due in the week of 16 November; exact day not confirmed)
catalysts.rationale: September NODX rose 68.4% y/y with electronics up 107.6%. Another strong print would confirm the surplus behind the strategic Bearish view and support the trade-weighted Singapore dollar. A slowdown below +20% would be the first sign that the AI export cycle is turning.

catalysts.event: FOMC minutes of the 27-28 October meeting
catalysts.rationale: The minutes will show how many participants besides the two dissenters favoured a hike. Wording such as 'many' or 'most' would push December odds towards 90% and reinforce the rate premium that carries the tactical score.

catalysts.event: Singapore October CPI and MAS core inflation, with MTI's final Q3 GDP, 2027 growth forecast and Q3 balance of payments (due in the week of 23 November; exact days not confirmed)
catalysts.rationale: Core inflation eased to 2.0% in September. A rise towards 2.3% would revive expectations of MAS tightening and push the S$NEER towards the strong edge of the band. A print of 1.8% or lower would let it slide towards the centre, lifting the pair. A Q3 current account above Q2's S$37.08bn would support the strategic view.

The advance estimate showed 3.4% annualised growth. Revisions are usually small, but a downward revision to consumption would temper the US growth story at a time when Singapore is growing faster, trimming the dollar's support into the December meeting.

catalysts.event: FOMC decision with Summary of Economic Projections
catalysts.rationale: A 25bp hike to 4.00-4.25% is 77-85% priced. The projections will decide whether the market's 4.7% path for 2027 survives. A hike with projections signalling a hold would lower the pair through the dollar's rate premium; higher dots would lift it and widen the money-market gap to SORA towards 280-300bp.

catalysts.event: Expiry of the continuing resolution funding the US government
catalysts.rationale: The stopgap signed on 2 September runs out on 11 December. A lapse would delay US data and raise fiscal risk premia on US assets without lifting policy expectations, which weakens the dollar against a AAA-surplus currency like the Singapore dollar.

catalysts.event: Year-end dollar funding and balance-sheet turn
catalysts.rationale: With reserves below USD 2.9tn and the TGA above USD 1tn, year-end demand for dollars should push SOFR above the rate paid on reserves and raise offshore dollar funding costs. That feeds quickly into Singapore's Asian dollar market and USD/SGD forwards, until the TGA falls back in January.

catalysts.event: MAS January Monetary Policy Statement (late January expected; date not confirmed)
catalysts.rationale: BofA expects a calibrated tightening in January 2027, while MUFG expects MAS to keep the current stance unless the medium-term inflation outlook changes materially. Forwards price no change, so any slope increase would pull the pair towards the 1.2628-1.2740 support band within weeks. A reduction, which is less likely, would send it back towards 1.30.

assumptions: Price data are daily closing prices with daily highs and lows: 130 weekday sessions from 2026-05-04 to 2026-10-30. Spot is 1.27819 at the 30 October close.
The valuation date is Sunday 1 November 2026. The gap to the spot date is the weekend only, with no trading sessions missed, and every level, distance and pip figure is anchored to 1.27819.

Moving averages and support/resistance zones are computed from 4,921 weekday sessions between 21 December 2007 and 30 October 2026 (1,011 weekly and 464 monthly bars). The 50-, 100- and 200-day and 200-week averages are simple averages of trading-day closes.
Realised volatility is annualised on 252 trading days. ATR(14) is 35 pips.

Only six resistance zones and one support zone met the two-touch threshold. Support below the 1.2628-1.2740 band is filled in with round numbers (1.2600, 1.2500) and the 52-week extremes (closing low 1.26139, intraday low 1.25883), flagged in the text as not computed zones.
The US 10-year yield on the monthly series is 4.99% as of September and is not a live level; the daily close of 4.98% on 29 October is used where a current figure is needed.
Singapore has no policy rate and no official 10-year series. Three-month compounded SORA of 1.297% is the Singapore short rate, giving a gap of about 258bp to the Fed mid-point of 3.875%.

No exchange lists an option or future on the Singapore dollar. Implied volatility, risk reversals, the term structure, a carry-to-implied-volatility ratio and a measured forward funding differential are therefore left blank, not estimated. Forward points are indicative bank quotes from 12 October and are labelled as such.

The factor stances rest on rates, macro data, positioning, trade, policy communication, cross-asset and geopolitical evidence. Recent price action was not used for any factor except Market Structure & Volatility, which draws on realised volatility and the band structure. Price levels are used only for entries, targets, stops, invalidators and sizing.
The S$NEER position (about 1.65% above mid, OCBC) and the slope (about 1.25% a year, UOB, 29 July) are bank estimates of an undisclosed band.

Bilateral goods trade is IMF data for 2024: US exports to Singapore $46.0bn, US imports from Singapore $43.2bn, a US surplus of $2.8bn. Singapore's own figures show exports to the US of $44.1bn and imports from the US of $55.9bn.

Singapore release dates for November, and MAS's January statement, are given as weeks because exact dates were not confirmed; the catalyst dates 2026-11-16, 2026-11-23 and 2027-01-28 are placeholders within those weeks.
Scenario probabilities and target levels are our own. Position sizes are illustrative risk-unit examples, not recommendations for any specific account.
The dossier dates in the metadata are set to the valuation date; the report does not state them separately.
